Cheesecakes in Singapore can be found just about anywhere, but they’re not quite the same as the silky delights from Tokyo’s Mr. Cheesecake. With over a million cheesecakes sold in Japan, these masterfully crafted desserts come from chef Koji Tamura. Through the art of Japanese precision, the humble cheesecake has been given a massive upgrade. But what makes Mr. Cheesecake’s desserts so worth the wait? Here’s the 411.
Mr. Cheesecake’s pop-up in Singapore: Details at a glance
When: 11 November to 30 December 2026
Price: TBC
Opening hours: TBC
Where: Mr. Cheesecake’s pop-up , Ion Orchard, opposite Hermes, Level 3, 2 Orchard Turn, Singapore 238801
What makes Mr. Cheesecake special
Photography: Mr. Cheesecake
From classic cheesecakes and burnt Basque cheesecakes to other dessert options like roll cakes, tiramisu, and financiers, Mr. Cheesecake’s offerings are nothing out of the ordinary. So what is it about these cakes that made this brand go insanely viral in Tokyo?
Part of Mr. Cheesecake’s uniqueness is in the method of serving. Its signature cheesecake has three different taste profiles, depending on the temperature you serve it. You can enjoy it frozen, where it’s extra tart and tastes like ice cream cake. Wait a little while for it to warm up and you get a contrast of textures with a smooth outer layer and frozen centre. Or have it fully thawed for a mouthfeel akin to creme brulee – the best way to enjoy the sweetness and aroma.
Mr. Cheesecake’s key flavours also read like a perfume list in the best way possible. Made with vanilla, white chocolate, tonka bean, and lemon, it’s skillfully balanced to create a rich but light cake.
And as Mr. Cheesecake says: it may not be the best in the world, but it might just be the best you’ll ever have in your life.
What to expect at the Singapore pop-up
Photography: Mr. Cheesecake
Very few details have been released about the brand’s upcoming Singapore pop-up. Given that it is the brand’s first-ever pop-up in Southeast Asia, we’re expecting minimalist displays that shine the spotlight on the main star – the cheesecakes.
We’re told to expect a curated line-up of five creations, brought together for the first time just for the Singapore debut. Flavours you can look forward to include the matcha and caramel Earl Grey cheesecakes and the rich tiramisu.
We’ll be back with more updates as more information rolls out, so stay tuned!
Frequently Asked Questions
What is Mr. Cheesecake?
It's a brand founded in 2018 by chef Koji Tamura. Mr. Cheesecake is best known for its (you guessed it) cheesecakes with rich and creamy flavour.
Why is it so popular?
Thanks to its distinct texture and layered flavours, Mr. Cheesecake is exceptionally popular in Japan. You can enjoy the cake at three different temperatures, and each has its unique texture and flavour.
Where is the Mr. Cheesecake pop-up?
It'll be located within Ion Orchard.
Is this Mr. Cheesecake's first pop-up?
Yes, this is the brand's inaugural pop-up in Southeast Asia.
Will this be permanent?
As far as we've heard, Mr. Cheesecake has no plans on opening a permanent store in Singapore.

Third Floor Singapore has opened on the rooftop of Design Orchard at 250 Orchard Road. It is an all-day neighbourhood bar from the team behind award-winning No Sleep Club, with cocktails, wine, coffee, food and music in a relaxed, living-room-inspired setting.
Image: Third Floor
Third Floor Singapore: a casual take on No Sleep Club
Overlooking Orchard Road, Third Floor brings the creativity and technical precision of No Sleep Club, which ranked No. 8 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars 2021 and No. 26 on The World’s 50 Best Bars 2021, into a more everyday space. Think comfortable seating, an open kitchen and bar, and a pace that suits morning coffee, casual lunches, afternoon drinks and evenings with friends.
Image: Third Floor
Founder Juan Yi Jun, who was born and raised in Singapore, says the name comes from her teenage years hanging out around Orchard. “The location became the name, and more importantly, it became ours,” she says. Her career took her through Tippling Club and Operation Dagger before she co-founded No Sleep Club.
Image: Third Floor
Cocktails worth ordering
Drinks start with a memory, an observation or a familiar ritual rather than a spirit. Jun’s graphic design training shapes how ideas are developed, with distillation, fermentation and clarification used to serve the idea, not to show off. Three drinks to look out for:
• Jolly Shandy: a beer-and-lime shandy poured over frozen house-made lime sherbet made from leftover citrus shells and peels, which you stir with a spoon.
• 3 Lime Vodka Soda: calamansi, kaffir lime leaf and Thai sweet lime with a citrus-hop distillate.
• Blue Cheese & Olive: a dirty martini with Stilton-infused gin, fino sherry, vermouth and a house-made tomato concentrate, finished with Gordal olives stuffed with blue cheese cream.
Image: Third Floor / Juan Qian
A place to return to
Beyond cocktails, Third Floor serves coffee, food, wine and beer through the day. Music and creative collaborations are part of the plan too. Events such as Void Deck Jam, which we covered when it stepped into Design Orchard on 4 October , bring DJs, independent food vendors and local collaborators together without losing the informality of a neighbourhood bar.
Image: Third Floor / Juan Qian
As Jun puts it: “We take what we do seriously, but that doesn’t mean our guests have to.”

Woksta has wok hei pasta from $7 in Bukit Merah
You’d typically expect pasta with bold flavours and bougie plating to only be found at atas Italian restaurants , but Woksta proves otherwise. This hawker stall at ABC Brickworks Market & Food Centre in Bukit Merah has gone viral for its wok-fried pasta that blends the beloved noodle dish with local flavours.
The stall is run by Chef Henry Yong, who used to work at Michelin-approved Scandinavian restaurant Dill. He swapped out the fine dining life for a hawker stall where he can spend more time with his family and return to his first love: cooking with a wok. Despite opening only about a month ago, Woksta has gained traction for their unique local take on pasta, and we had to see if the food was worth the hype.
Woksta’s menu is straightforward, with only three choices available , each plated beautifully and paired with their signature coconut sauce that’s made in-store.
Living up to their name, all their pasta is fried with a wok to achieve wok hei, AKA that char and smoky depth of flavour.
We started our pasta feast with the Curry Fried Chicken ($7) , which was served with generous chunks of fried chicken and a medley of vegetables, including capsicum, zucchini, and onions.
Initially, I was sceptical about how the coconut sauce would pair with the various noodle dishes, but it actually blended well with the curry flavour from the noodles. The sauce was silky smooth and added a lemak touch to the dish, reminiscent of coconut milk.
This dish had the strongest wok hei, as you can see from the char on each strand of pasta.
Each chicken chunk was generously coated with curry powder, adding a subtly spicy kick in each crunchy bite.
Next we tried the Fish & Coconut ($9) . Unlike the other two variations where the coconut sauce is plated on the side, the noodles here were completely doused in the sauce. The sauce was creamy and had a strong coconut taste that was not too cloying. I liked how the onions added a nice crunch to cut through the richness, while also adding a natural sweetness.
In terms of wok hei, this dish didn’t quite have a strong char as it was creamier than the rest, but it was still pleasant to eat.
Though it looks a bit like batang fish at first glance, the fish used here is seabass, fried until golden brown for a crispy exterior. The fish itself was flaky, though it did taste a tad fishy.
Last but not least is the Laksa Seafood ($10) , which turned out to be my favourite of the lot. Though it didn’t taste entirely like laksa, I enjoyed the subtle floral note from the laksa leaves on top and the crunch from the veggies.
The sauce also had a hint of spiciness from the chilli oil. I recommend mixing it all up to marry the flavours.
As a seafood lover, I appreciated the generous portions of both prawns and sotong, which were plump and QQ, giving the dish more texture and mouthfeel.
Overall, I’d say that the food did live up to the hype. I could taste Chef Henry’s heart in each dish, and it’s definitely worth heading down to give it a try for yourself. Do note that they’re only open for three hours per day, so it’s best to come early to beat the lunch crowd.

Osteria Da Su opens at 163 Telok Ayer Street on Friday 23 October 2026, with 25 sharing plates from S$14++ that fold Korean accents into classic Italian cooking. The casual osteria is the newest restaurant from NAE:UM Group , next door to its one-Michelin-starred Korean fine-dining sibling NAE:UM, and is run by Korea-born Chef Suji Park.
Photo: Osteria Da Su
Opening week is dinner only. From 16 November the kitchen plans Monday to Saturday lunch and dinner. Bookings go through the restaurant’s reservation link at bit.ly/dasu.
Who is cooking
Park has cooked Italian food for close to 20 years, including stints in Bergamo, Milan and Sicily, three years at three-Michelin-starred Da Vittorio in Bergamo, two years at Claudio Sadler’s Milan trattoria, and time on the opening team of Massimo Bottura’s Gucci Osteria in Seoul. She and NAE:UM chef founder Louis Han met as students at Korea Tourism College and have been friends for 16 years. The Telok Ayer unit next to NAE:UM came up for lease in June 2026, and they opened the Italian room together.
The name works in two languages. In Italian, “da Su” reads as an osteria from Su. In Korean, “da su” means many people, which is how the kitchen frames a neighbourhood table rather than a tasting counter.
What is on the menu
Handmade pasta sits at the centre of the list. Spaghetti alle vongole is S$28++, built on asari clam stock with Korean water parsley (minari) in place of Italian parsley, and the shells removed before service. Tortelli di galbi jjim is S$30++, with Korean braised pork inside handmade tortelli and sage butter. Farfalle all’amatriciana is S$24++, finished with guanciale chips brushed in gochujang bulgogi sauce.
Photo: Osteria Da Su
Smaller plates start lower. Korean pepper fritto, a fried gochu chilli stuffed with prawn and ricotta and served with doenjang mayonnaise and balsamic soy, is S$14++. Zucchini bruschetta is S$12++, and insalata condiglione with a Korean soy-marinated egg is S$18++. For dessert, dalgona tiramisu is S$14++, a classic mascarpone and savoiardi tiramisu topped with housemade dalgona honeycomb, and salame di cioccolato is S$10++.
Photo: Osteria Da Su
The room
The restaurant seats 34: eight at the kitchen counter, 16 on banquettes and ten in a raised lounge. The fit-out mixes arched openings, terracotta floors and warm wood with a cleaner Korean line, and framed photographs Park took in Italy hang on the walls. Diners walk past the open kitchen on the way in.
Telok Ayer Street is a short walk from Telok Ayer and Downtown MRT stations. The group’s other sibling restaurant is GU:UM, a modern Korean steakhouse, which makes the Italian room its first non-Korean concept in Singapore. Prices carry a 10 per cent service charge and GST. The restaurant is not halal-certified.

Rawr Cafe is a new tiger-themed cafe in Jalan Besar
Wunderfolks , the mastermind behind Oh Wunder Cafe and Cafe Barco , is back with another concept. Its latest venture, Rawr Cafe , opened in Jalan Besar on 17 October 2027 . Unlike the other two concepts, this new cafe offers locally inspired brunch fare in a cute tiger-themed setup.
The cafe interior features adorable red-and-white tiger graphics.
You’ll also find a display of merchandise, from their house-made kaya to a tiger-inspired cap and stickers.
The menu features local flavours in the form of Western brunch classics. Some must-tries recommended by the cafe are the Singaporean Breakfast Latte ($8++) , Nasi Lemak Chicken Burger ($18++), Laksa Cream Halibut ($24++), Gula Melaka Pandan Cloud ($8++), Tiger Bomb ($12++), and Soft Shell Crab Chilli Pasta ($23++).
The Soft Shell Crab Chilli Pasta was served with a whole crab. The tomato-based sauce was sweet, tangy, and mildly spicy. Personally, it tasted more like regular red pasta sauce than chilli crab.
The soft-shell crab appeared to be lightly battered and deep-fried, giving it a crispy exterior. Beneath the shell was tender, fleshy crab meat with some creamy roe. The crab had some natural sweetness and brininess that came through nicely.
The Nasi Lemak Chicken Burger was extremely hearty, layered with fried chicken, fresh lettuce, and cucumber, then topped with ikan bilis and sambal for that bold umami flavour.
For sides, we got the Prawn Paste Chicken ($15++) . It tasted like regular har cheong gai—the exterior was fried till crisp, coating the greasy, tender chicken wing. I noticed that the chicken meat was a little pinker than what I was used to, so I thought it could’ve been cooked for longer.
We also got two of the signature drinks: the SG Breakfast Latte, a creamy pandan latte, and Tiger Bomb, espresso topped with orange foam.
Image credit: Rawr Cafe
You can also choose to top your drinks with an adorable Raw Tiger Cookie Topper for just $2++!
The SG Breakfast Latte caught our eye with its e foamy “fried egg” on top. It’s served with a crunchy slab of kaya toast, which was light, fragrant, and perfect for soaking up the latte. FYI: the “yolk” in the foam is kaya-flavoured!
The Tiger Bomb had an intense citrusy flavour, thanks to the addition of the orange-infused foam. Paired with espresso, it made for a unique flavour combination that’s worth trying.
Overall, Rawr Cafe is definitely worth a visit if you love cutesy cafes. The SG Breakfast Latte is my favourite in terms of taste and appearance, so give it a go!

Casa Vostra is opening at Wisma Atria with famous pizza
Fans of Italian food would likely already be familiar with Casa Vostra . When they first opened at Raffles City back in 2024, the queues stretched out the door—some waiting over an hour just to get a table. Since then, they’ve expanded to JEM and Tampines Mall , giving more diners a chance to try their offerings.
Image credit: Casa Vostra
If you still haven’t made the trip, good news: Casa Vostra is opening their fourth outlet at Wisma Atria , so those who work in the area can get a taste of their new outlet-exclusive menu items. Look forward to their trademarked Roman SquareCrunch Pizza , as well as mascarpone gelato served in a crunchy pastry cone, in collaboration with Mediterranean-Levantine restaurant Petra.
We Visited Casa Vostra Again To See If The Italian Restaurant Fared Better
For those unfamiliar, Casa Vostra is a casual Italian dining concept by Mission Group and Chef Antonio Miscellaneo, the same chef behind La Bottega Enoteca, which is widely regarded as Singapore’s top pizzeria.
What makes the food here different is how it’s made. The pizza dough is cold-fermented and the pasta hand-rolled, with ingredients either sourced directly from Italy or made in-house. Their pizzas come in three styles: Newpolitan Red , which has a San Marzano tomato base, Newpolitan White , featuring a cheese base, and the Doublecrunch , essentially a pizza-sandwich hybrid.
When we visited their OG outlet in 2025, we tried the Peposo ($22++) —braised beef cheek served with rosemary roasted potatoes and finished with black pepper. We also enjoyed the Crab Tagliatelle ($26++) , generously loaded with sweet crab flesh and tossed in a savoury mix of olive oil, garlic, and butter.
On the pizza side, the Tartufo e Funghi ($28++) is a must for truffle fans, topped with fresh black truffle, mushrooms, and a drizzle of truffle oil over a base of Fior di Latte and Taleggio. And if you’re in the mood for something sweet and savoury, the Prosciutto e Figura ($27++) —Parma ham, fig puree, rocket and walnuts on freshly baked dough—holds its own as one of the best pies on the menu.
The new outlet boasts an 85-seater open-plan space, perfect for date nights or a meal out with the fam. Do note that the restaurant operates on a walk-in only basis, so it’s best to head down early to beat the queue.

Have you passed by Spicy Hubby at Centrepoint Food Street and realised that the stall’s name rings a bell? That’s because it belongs to the same founder who owns Spicy Wife , a popular Malaysian-style nasi lemak stall at Amoy Street Food Centre that attracts long snaking queues during lunchtime.
Boasting a retro charm, the 60-seater eatery evokes the nostalgic vibe of Heap Seng Leong Coffeeshop with its signature blue-and-white tiled walls. Besides its faux retro-style windows, the space even displays old-fashioned toys and snacks for sale, just like those mama stalls that I frequented when I was still in primary school. Everything is self-service here, from placing your order at the kiosk to collecting your food.
What to order at Spicy Hubby
We started off with one of their new additions — the Nasi Ayam Gepuk (S$12.90) . A bed of nasi lemak was crowned with a whole battered chicken thigh that’s drizzled with kicap manis , served with a sunny-side-up, peanut gravy and sambal .
Just look at how glorious that chicken thigh was! Ginormous and coated in a golden-brown batter that didn’t look overly greasy, the chicken definitely made a great first impression. Unfortunately, the meat itself was devoid of any seasoning. It was only when enjoyed with the skin that the faint, sweet notes of the kicap manis truly came through.
However, pairing the chicken with the peanut sauce and s ambal combo was a game-changer in the best way possible. The peanut sauce that reminded me of the thick renditions served at hotpot places was rich and nutty, while the shiok , fiery sambal came in hot and ready to rumble. Try them together for yourself — you’ll get exactly what I mean! The rice was equally well executed, with fluffy grains and a robust coconut fragrance that tied everything nicely.
Next on our agenda was the other new kid on the block — the Nasi Rendang Ayam (S$12.90) . Sitting alongside the nasi lemak was a generous portion of chicken rendang pieces sprinkled with desicated coconut, accompanied by prawn keropok and a fried egg.
The rendang doesn’t taste like the usual ones that I have at nasi padang spots. It was saucy and undeniably unique, in a good way, with an interesting enough flavour that kept me going back for more. Those who don’t particularly enjoy fried food in general might prefer this more.
Of course, we had to get the signature Nasi Goreng Ayam Berempah (S$9.90) , a dish that made them popular at their flagship CBD hawker stall. This nasi lemak combo with a whole slab of spiced fried chicken was slightly more traditional than the other two. It came with the usual ikan bilis -peanut combo, fried egg, and sambal .
My dining partners had visited Spicy Wife before, but this was my first time trying it. Compared to the earlier Nasi Ayam Gepuk , this rendition boasted a far superior marinade. The flesh was well-seasoned, while the crispy skin was infused with an aromatic array of spices that added a ton of flavour without overwhelming the palate. The few pieces of fried curry leaves also gave an extra boost of fragrance to the chicken.
The sambal might’ve looked intimidating by its colour, but it’s actually mild with a slight hint of sweetness.
We also tried a number of their sides. The XL Otak (S$4.90) , Long Bean Sambal (S$4.90) , and Curry Fish Ball (S$6.90) .
My favourite was the Curry Fish Ball , which had a flavoursome curry and QQ fishballs. It may not look like much, but give me anything with curry and I’ll polish everything off. It tasted like the ones I had on my last Hong Kong trip. As for the XL Otak , it fell a little flat in the flavour department. If only the fish paste and spices were a tad stronger; it would’ve been much better.

Who Spicy Hubby is best for

Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup , the Geylang shop that has sold turtle soup since 1946, has opened its first mall outlet at Great World this month, in the year the family business turns 80.
The new restaurant sits at #B1-106/107, 1 Kim Seng Promenade. It opens daily from 11am to 10pm, with last order at 9.30pm, and closes only for Chinese New Year. Great World MRT on the Thomson-East Coast Line (TE15) is the easy way in: Exit 6 leads into the mall at Basement 2, and the restaurant is one floor up.
Claypot Turtle Soup, the house signature since 1986. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
From a shoulder pole to Lorong Bachok
The family traces its roots to Fengtang Xiang in Chao’an. Tan Ah Sai arrived in Singapore in 1927, aged 11, and after the war cooked herbal turtle soup for workers rebuilding the city, selling it bowl by bowl from a shoulder-pole pushcart before saving for a tricycle. He founded the business in 1946.
His son Tan Khar Seng took over the fire in 1973, at 20, while supporting eight siblings, and his wife Tay Ah Lek cooked through the night. In 1986 the shop moved to individual claypots, which the family bills as Singapore’s first claypot turtle soup. It settled at 29 Lorong Bachok in 1992, and the third generation, Vivian and Allan, joined in the 2000s.
The Tan family, photographed in a Singapore studio in the 1960s. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
What a bowl costs
The family publishes dine-in prices for the Geylang shop and has not posted a separate Great World menu, so treat these as the reference point rather than a promise for Kim Seng Promenade.
• Claypot Turtle Soup: S$28 small, S$50 medium, S$78 large
• Double Boiled Turtle Soup: S$16 small, S$21 medium
• Premier Fish Maw and Abalone Soup: S$30
• Ginseng Black Chicken Soup and Cordyceps Chicken Soup: S$15 each
• Sugarcane, Water Chestnut and Imperatae Root Soup: S$9.90
The double-boiled small bowl is the cheapest way into the turtle soups. Sides run from S$6 for cucumber in vinaigrette to S$16.90 for steamed seabass with Teochew olive vegetable, and a bowl of Fragrant Yam Rice is S$2.50. The menu does not state whether service charge or GST applies. Prices on GrabFood, foodpanda and Oddle run higher than in the shop.
Double Boiled Turtle Soup, from S$16 at the Geylang shop. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
Cordyceps Chicken Soup, S$15 at the Geylang shop. Photo: Tan Ser Seng Herbal Soup
Before you go
There are no table reservations at either branch. Seating is walk-in, first come, first served. The Great World outlet takes WhatsApp messages only, on 8997 0368. Pick-up orders and food reservations go through a separate WhatsApp line, 8737 2929, and food is set aside once paid.
Tan Ser Seng is not halal-certified. It serves pork dishes, and some soups carry a splash of house herbal wine. The family describes its soups in traditional terms and is clear that the descriptions are not medical advice.
The original shop at 29 Lorong Bachok keeps shorter hours, 11am to 8.30pm daily with last order at 8pm, a five-minute walk from Aljunied MRT.

Island Penang Kitchen at 721 Clementi West Street 2 was an accidental discovery when I visited the West Coast neighbourhood. The eatery seemed popular, judging from the long line that had formed, so I made a mental note to visit them in the near future.
I also texted my relatives who live in the neighbourhood, and found out that they found the food to be quite good. Since it has been a while since I last had Penang food , I decided to pay them a visit at 11.30am before the lunch crowd arrived. True enough, it was relatively empty— hooray!
What I tried at Island Penang Kitchen
I started with one of my favourite appetisers, the Penang Rojak (Fruits & You Tiao ) for S$7 . I was more inclined on this although they had another variation that had you tiao only at the same price.
My first impression— the generous sprinkling of peanuts— a plus for someone like me who loves nuts in all forms ( ahem … don’t let your imagination run wild).
As for the ingredients, there were pieces of Japanese cucumber, turnip, you tiao and pineapple. But wait, is pineapple the only fruit ? I was a little confused since the combination was similar to a typical local rendition, except for the missing tau pok . I was expecting fruits like jambu to appear.
Nonetheless, I decided to go for it. The pieces of you tiao were super crispy and, most importantly, not hard. The pineapple was sweet and the turnip and cucumber gave varying levels of texture and crunch.
The hei ko sauce was seasoned to perfection and coated the ingredients evenly. Overall, I was pretty satisfied. This was a good start!
Instead of getting the iconic Penang Fried Kway Teow (S$7.80) , I decided to switch things up and ordered the Penang Fried Mi Tai Mak (S$7.80) instead. When the dish arrived, we were immediately captivated by its smoky fragrance.
The ‘rat tails’ were stir fried with slices of Chinese sausage, 2 peeled prawns, bean sprouts, fish cake slices and chives.
The noodles tasted as delicious as they smelled, each strand possessing a robust punch of wok hei smokiness. Although the chilli packed some heat, it still allowed me to taste the other components of the dish without numbing my tongue.

The prawns were decent and firm, while the strands of tau geh retained a satisfying crunch. We also found mini golden nuggets of pork lard, hiding like bats hibernating in a cave. My only gripe? They were inconsistent— some were crispy and delicious, while others were slightly chewy and soft.
My favourite component of the Penang Fried Mi Tai Mak was the red slices of lap cheong , which injected subtly sweet and savoury notes throughout the dish.
We then shifted our attention to the bowl of Penang Assam Laksa (S$6.80) . The noodles were topped with bits of fish, sliced lettuce, mint leaves and chunks of pineapple.
The noodles used weren’t thick bee hoon but lai fun , which were slightly thicker and had a translucent appearance. It’s the same kind of noodles used in Penang, too— 100 points for authenticity!
The broth was gently tangy but I could hardly taste the umami -ness of the hei ko . Thankfully, we were given a bottle of shrimp paste sauce to enhance the flavour. I added about a full tablespoon of it, and that really helped to redeem the dish.
Initially, we debated whether the fish bits were ikan kembung (mackerel) or sardines, but we leaned towards the former due to its taste and texture. It added a depth of richness to the bowl of laksa .
The slices of pineapple gave the dish a mild sweetness while the mint leaves made things more herby and aromatic.
Since we always reserve a small compartment in our bellies for dessert , we shared a bowl of Penang Homemade Chendol (S$3.50) . Instead of red beans, kidney beans were used alongside the quintessential pandan jelly strands.
After giving it a good mix, the gula melaka at the bottom gradually turned everything a light brown hue. The taste was decent and satisfying, but it was similar to any other chendo l we had tried before— nothing to shout about.
Final thoughts
Overall, we were quite satisfied with the Penang dishes served at Island Penang Kitchen. Although there were some hits and misses, the positives outweigh the negatives.
With a decent menu, reasonable prices, and tasty dishes, I finally understood the appeal and popularity of this eatery, even though it’s tucked away in the back of the heartland neighbourhood where many might overlook it.
I guess from now on, if I’m craving Penang food, this place will be one of my top choices and recommendations.

Habibi Kebs has affordable doner kebabs in Kembangan
Doner kebabs are low-key an underrated option for a fast and affordable meal : they’re quick to prepare, portable, and packed full of vegetables for your daily dose of vitamins. So, next time you’re in Kembangan running errands or passing by on your daily jog along the park connectors, check out Habibi Kebs , a Muslim-owned eatery serving Berlin-inspired doner kebabs at nett prices.
Food at Habibi Kebs
For the uninitiated: doner kebabs are a traditional Turkish dish. The word “doner” comes from the Turkish term “dönmek”, meaning to “turn” or “rotate”, which aptly describes how it’s cooked: seasoned meat, usually chicken, beef, or lamb, is stacked on a vertical rotisserie and cooked until crispy on the outside and juicy within.
Habibi Kebs is a no-frills store specialising in authentic doner kebabs. The founders shared with us that they both have had prior culinary experience, and after a hiatus, they both decided to come together to start Habibi Kebs to bring the German doner experience to the masses. Contrary to traditional Turkish doner that’s served with rice, grilled vegetables, or tombik (AKA Turkish round pocket loaf) with little sauces and salads, German doner goes heavy on salad and sauces: all dressed and packed into bread for a portable, street-food-style sandwich.
The menu’s pretty straightforward: choose from three main styles, your protein of chicken, beef, or a mix of both, and a sauce: Garlic Sauce , Chili Sauce , or Herb Sauce . If you want it more saucy, you can top up $1 for an additional sauce.
If you’re feeling peckish, you can even upgrade your meal for an additional $5 , which comes with a side of fries and a soft drink.
We first got their signature Chicken Doner Kebab with Garlic and Chili Sauce ($11) . You get doner bread, AKA Turkish flatbread, stuffed with lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and chicken, dressed in a spicy chilli and zingy garlic sauce.
The doner bread had a nice crusty exterior and a soft, fluffy interior, making the perfect base for the whole dish. The chicken was well marinated and slightly smoky, which complemented the fresh vegetables.
We also tried their Beef Durum with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($11) , which featured the same medley of lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and grilled minced beef, drenched in a zingy garlic and herb sauce. The whole shebang was tightly wrapped in durum bread, similar to a burrito you’d get from Stuff’d.
The minced beef was nicely charred and finely minced, while the vegetables helped cut through some of its richness. I particularly liked how the durum was left under a press grill for a while, giving it a crunchy exterior for some textural contrast.
Worth noting: the owner mentioned that the minced beef is likely being phased out soon, so head down sooner rather than later if you want to try this combo.
Last but not least, we ordered the Mixed Doner Teller with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($14) . It featured a bed of golden-brown, thick-cut fries loaded with both aforementioned meats, lettuce, jalapenos, tomatoes, red cabbage, and red onions, then finished with a drizzle of garlic and herb sauces.
Usually, I’m wary of loaded fries as they tend to turn soggy fast. However, the fries here were still crispy on the outside and fluffy on the inside. They were generously loaded with toppings, and I particularly enjoyed how the vegetables and herb sauce helped to mellow out the richness.
We also had the opportunity to try one of their unreleased items: the Quesadilla ($12) , which featured doner chicken, mozzarella, and chili sauce encased in a tortilla wrap, and grilled till crunchy on the outside.
Without a doubt, this was our favourite dish of the bunch: cheesy and creamy, with a little kick from the chili sauce.
The release date is currently TBD, though the owner told us it could be as early as this month. So, do keep a lookout on their Instagram page for any updates.
Finally, we washed it all down with Salaam Cola ($3) , a soft drink hailing from Ireland that was refreshing on a hot day. It was sweet and fizzy, and tasted similar to Coke. The brand that produces Salaam Cola also donates 10% of their profits to conflict-afflicted regions.
Ambience at Habibi Kebs
The eatery is decked out in a vibrant red-and-white aesthetic reminiscent of an American diner. If you’re dining in, there are also a few chairs outside so you can sit down and enjoy your meal. You’ll definitely need it, as the interior of the store itself is squeezy with little ventilation, which isn’t an ideal condition for you to enjoy a sandwich in.
When we visited the store on a weekday lunch, there wasn’t much of a crowd, so we didn’t need to wait much for our food to arrive. However, the traffic did start to pick up after we got our food, so do come early if you’d like to skip the queue.
Habibi Kebs is located a five-minute walk from Kembangan MRT Station .

Nomad Kitchen is a new stall at Taman Jurong
Finding quality Middle Eastern fare in Singapore isn’t always easy. But a stall serving dishes from Iran, Turkey, Italy, Greece, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, and Afghanistan? That’s even harder to come by. So when we came across Nomad Kitchen , we knew we had to check it out.
Located in Taman Jurong Market and Food Centre , the new stall has already earned itself a solid reputation, reportedly selling out daily. Its founder, Fuad Salim, a self-professed F&B nomad, picked up the recipes throughout his 30-year career in hospitality, where he worked as an F&B and hotel manager.
Food at Nomad Kitchen
The menu consists of Afghan Chicken (from $6) from Afghanistan, Saffron Jujeh ($8) from Iran, Iskender ($12) from Turkey, Shakshuka ($7) from Morocco, Lasagna ($8.50) from Italy, Moussaka ($8) from Greece, and finally, rotisserie chicken and street wraps inspired by Saudi Arabia.
Chef Fuad prepares everything from scratch daily, including handmade Lavash flatbreads, grilled meats, kabuli rice, saffron rice, and lasagna.
We started with the $6 portion of Afghan Chicken. For an extra $2.50 , you can get another quarter of the rotisserie chicken, which we thought was extremely generous in this economy.
While I tend to find roast chicken too dry for my liking, this one was juicy, moist, and expertly cooked. The seasoning was flavourful too, with a blend of spices that added depth without being overly salty. However, we found the white meat slightly bland, as most of the seasoning was concentrated on the skin and hadn’t penetrated the meat.
According to the chef, raisins and carrots are integral to an Afghan kabuli rice dish. I could see why: they added a burst of sweetness to the aromatic rice, making for a complex and layered flavour profile.
The Saffron Jujeh was probably my favourite dish—it came with two chunky grilled chicken kebabs, saffron rice, roasted tomatoes and peppers, and a yoghurt sauce. Again, the generous portion size was a pleasant surprise.
The kebabs had a similarly intense spice blend to the rotisserie; however, they were thoroughly marinated, so every bite was full of flavour. The yoghurt-based sauce was tangy and refreshing, but more subtle, which worked well to highlight the kebab rather than overpower it.
The roasted vegetables were smoky and juicy, and good enough to stand alone as a side dish. Traditionally, though, Persians would mash the juicy tomatoes into saffron rice, turning them into a flavourful “sauce”.
Lastly, we tried the lasagna. Most faux-Italian places I know of put an ungodly amount of cheese on their lasagna (I’m not complaining). This one was more well-balanced, with all the elements complementing each other rather than overpowering the dish.
The pasta sheets were quite thick and satisfyingly chewy. They made for a great vessel for the layers of beef ragu, Neapolitan sauce, and bechamel. The dish was savoury and hearty, with hints of sweetness and acidity to balance it out.
Ambience at Nomad Kitchen
Nomad Kitchen is tucked away in the corner of Taman Jurong Market and Food Centre. We arrived around 12:30pm to a short queue and a steady stream of customers.
The market itself was huge and happening, with three stories worth of food and retail stalls. It was relatively well-ventilated, with multiple fans working overtime to combat the Singapore stuffiness.
The market is a 10-minute bus ride or 18-minute walk from Lakeside MRT Station.
Nomad Kitchen – Eatbook Review
I visited Nomad Kitchen with high expectations, knowing Chef Fuad Salim’s hospitality background, and was still pleasantly surprised. Every element of the food was well-cooked and flavourful. The dishes also seemed to stay true to their cultural roots, with ingredients and flavours recreated as authentically as possible.
As a Westie, I will definitely be revisiting to try the rest of the menu.

Tokyo’s iconic dessert sensation, Mr. CHEESECAKE , is officially debuting in Singapore with an exclusive pop-up at ION Orchard from 11 Nov to 30 Dec 2026 . Founded by acclaimed Chef Koji Tamura, the cheesecake brand has achieved legendary status — selling over 1 million whole cakes globally.
Prior to establishing Mr. CHEESECAKE, Chef Tamura built a distinguished career at world-renowned fine-dining establishments, including Mirazur and Restaurant ES in France. He also served as head chef at Tokyo’s TIRPSE, which is famous for receiving a Michelin star in the shortest time in the world.
Despite his impressive resume, Chef Tamura was most inspired by childhood memories of his mother’s home-baked treats and his own experience of baking a cake for a high school friend’s birthday. He began crafting cheesecakes late at night and sharing them on social media. The overwhelming online response eventually led him to depart from fine-dining kitchens and launch Mr. CHEESECAKE.
What sets Mr. CHEESECAKE apart from other cheesecake brands is its signature dual-layer construction that consists of a delicately baked top layer paired with a velvety, near-rare bottom layer. This unique construction is deliberate, allowing the flavours, aroma and mouthfeel of the cake to evolve with temperature changes and provide different sensory experiences with the same cake:
Frozen: Enjoyed straight from the freezer for a refreshing, ice-cream-like bite.
Half-Thawed (1–1.5 hours): Offers a dual texture with a frozen centre wrapped in a creamy outer coat.
Fully Thawed: Unlocks rich sweetness and aroma with a silky consistency akin to creme brulee.
We got to sample Mr. CHEESECAKE Matcha (S$69) , RICH TIRAMISU (S$69) and Mr. CHEESECAKE Sakekasu Coconut (S$69), served fully thawed. Do note that cakes are only sold whole and portions pictured in my article are tasting samples.
My favourite cake by far was Mr. CHEESECAKE Sakekasu Coconut , which carried sweet and floral tropical notes. This unusual combination pairs sake kasu with rich coconut and uplifts it with a touch of lychee puree. The sake kasu , which is the leftover pressed lees from sake production, brings a mildly yeasty and tangy flavour — akin to yoghurt — to the cake.
This gentle acidity pairs well with the smooth, buttery profile of the coconut and pleasant floral aroma of lychee, making for a complex and layered profile with depth without feeling too heavy or sweet.
Another offering that I thoroughly enjoyed was Mr. CHEESECAKE Matcha (S$69) . It might be too intensely earthy for casual drinkers like me, but dedicated matcha lovers are bound to adore it. It also features light, creamy mascarpone and a dash of vanilla to balance the richness and slight bitterness of the matcha. Despite the bold flavours of this cake, it remains remarkably light and enjoyable with just the right level of sweetness.
Finally, we moved on to the RICH TIRAMISU (S$69). Rather than a purely traditional tiramisu, Mr. CHEESECAKE’s version incorporates Japanese ingredients like hojicha , which imparted an earthy, roasted aroma.
Building on that roasted aroma, the addition of browned butter lends more depth and a slight nuttiness to the overall profile. In the middle sits a thin, crisp almond dacquoise layer to provide a textural variation from the mousse-like interior. However, for a tiramisu, I found it rather lacking in coffee flavours.
Driven by Chef Tamura’s humble ethos — “Not the world’s best, but we make your days the best” — this limited-time pop-up brings one of Japan’s most coveted pastries to local dessert enthusiasts. Make sure to head down between 11 Nov and 30 Dec 2026 to get a taste of his renowned cheesecakes.

If you’re looking for another spot to add to your JB itinerary, this one’s worth checking out.
The current exchange rate is RM1 = ~S$0.31 as of 27 October 2026.

The cafe boasts a rustic Chinese look with traditional motifs and wooden furniture that’ll send you back to Season One of The Rise of Phoenixes . There are plenty of photo spots, so be sure to get your camera ready.
As aesthetic as the spot may be, they didn’t skimp on the quality of the desserts either. You can expect a wide variety of Chinese desserts, ranging from traditional classics to modern variants.
As a pistachio fanatic , their Pistachio Beancurd Mochi (RM15.90) was basically calling my name. Imagine a bowl filled generously with pistachio-flavoured tau huay, topped with stretchy mochi and cheese foam, then garnished with chopped pistachios.
This bowl met my rather high standards for pistachio desserts: it had prominent earthy, umami pistachio flavours, without being too sweet. The mochi also added a nice textural contrast—soft and stretchy with an indulgent milky taste. The cheese foam tied the whole dessert together, adding a subtle saltiness that offset the sweetness.
My dining companion preferred the Oh Yeah! Mollie (RM14.90) , comprising a base of coconut jelly piled high with toppings, including coconut milk he fen AKA Chinese wide noodles, rose-infused chestnuts, and fresh mango cubes. It’s then finished with a heaping scoop of coconut ice cream and a sprinkle of toasted coconut.
This dessert can be described in one word: refreshing. The coconut jelly is QQ and jiggly, and reminded me of the Chinese dessert bing fen.
The coconut ice cream, on the other hand, was soft and creamy. The fragrant coconut flavour was further accentuated by the coconut he fen, which tasted very similar to actual coconut meat.
The fresh mangoes were also slightly sour, cutting through the richness of the dessert, while the rose-infused chestnuts provided a nice crunch.
To wash everything down, we ordered the Taro Milk Tea With Mochi (RM15.80) , comprising Assam milk tea zhnged up with taro paste and handmade mochi, finished with a layer of cheese foam.
If you’re an orh nee lover , this drink is basically tailor-made for you. The Assam milk tea base was quite light and fragrant, allowing the stronger-tasting yam paste to come through. The mochi also added a nice bite: it was soft and slightly chewy, making it feel more like a dessert than a drink.
Interestingly, the dessert cafe offers a lineup of fresh shio pan. We ordered their Mentaiko Shio Pan (RM8.90) , and surprisingly, it could rival my favourite salt breads. It had a crunchy, buttery base, with a soft and chewy middle, and was garnished with mentaiko mayo, seaweed, and a slab of creamy Kewpie mayonnaise.
That’s not all: the bread is split lengthwise and slathered with more creamy mentaiko mayo for added umami.
Mollie Makes is located a seven-minute drive away from CIQ Jalan Jim Quee .

Potatoes are a beloved staple for many, myself included. With their versatility, you can cook them in so many ways — boiled, mashed, fried — you name it, it probably yields delicious results. If your favourite potato dish is rosti , you’ll be happy to hear that Hippopotato has opened its first physical store in Punggol .
Previously a popular home-based business selling a large variety of rosti with 5.0 stars across 516 Google reviews (at the time of writing), the owners have decided to open up shop in Northshore Plaza I . Their original home-based outlet in Tampines will be closed until further notice, with plans to resume business there once the Punggol store can run independently.
The rosti store is helmed by 2 brothers, Gary Wong and James Wong. Born into a family of cooks and hawkers, the brothers said in an Instagram post , “Food has always been a big part of our DNA”. Hence, they started Hippopotato in 2025 with the goal of making yummy rosti accessible to all.
Fun fact: They used to run a cai fan stall at a Junior College. Plus, James used to be a Marche chef at, you guessed it… the rosti station. Without further ado, here’s what I tried at Hippopotato.
I started with their Golden Classic Rosti (S$5) and opted for sour cream. The usual price for this is S$8 , but to celebrate their grand opening, the first 50 customers can get it for S$5 . This promotion runs from 15 to 18 Oct 2026 , while stocks last.
The rostis were made to order, thus having a perfectly crisp exterior with a nice char that added smokiness to every bite. The potatoes were soft and delicate on the interior, creating a nice medley of textures. When topped with the sour cream, it adds a piquancy to the mild dish. Personally, I prefer it with a heaping spoonful of the sour cream.
The next rosti I tried was the O konomirosti (S$10.50) . This dish is the lovechild of popular Japanese dish o konomiyaki and rosti , inheriting the positives of both parents. As you can see in the picture above, Hippopotato is extremely generous with the bonito flakes given.
Beneath the flakes are also generous drizzles of tangy okonomiyaki sauce and Japanese mayonnaise. This was my favourite as each bite just brought such intense goodness to my taste buds. Bold and savoury from the bonito flakes and okonomiyaki sauce, slightly creamy from the mayonnaise — just wow.
Aside from rosti , Hippopotato also has a range of potato-based sides, such as tater tots and fries. I opted for the Mentaiko Mayo Tater Tots (S$5) . I’m a huge mentaiko fan, but I find typical mentaiko sauces lack the same umami as the actual pollack roe.
Luckily for me, the sauce hits the spot. Slightly spicy with a rich, briny flavour, it complemented the crispy tater tots well. The only thing I wished for was more sauce; there’s an option for the sauce to be on the side for an additional S$0.30, which I will probably go for in the future.
Would I recommend Hippopotato ? Definitely. With amazing rosti and sides, why not #supportlocal while enjoying good food?

Tiger Remix is here, and Singapore gets it first. Tiger Beer has launched the flavoured lager range globally in Singapore and Malaysia, starting with two Asian-inspired flavours: Peach Oolong and Yuzu Lime.
Image: Tiger Beer
What is Tiger Remix?
Tiger Remix keeps the crisp, balanced character of the brand’s premium lager and adds a fruit-and-tea twist. Peach Oolong pairs juicy peach with aromatic oolong tea for a smooth finish, while Yuzu Lime combines zesty yuzu and tangy lime for a brighter, citrus-led sip. Both are described as low in bitterness, which should make them an easy first step for drinkers who find regular lager too sharp.
Both variants contain 4.2% ABV and come in 320ml cans.
Image: Tiger Beer
Street-culture design, local roots
The packaging leans on Asian street culture, with signboard-inspired typography, shophouse forms and motifs that reflect the region. Tiger was born in Singapore in 1932, and Magdalene Tan, Head of Marketing of Asia Pacific Breweries, said the debut here carries special significance: Singapore is shaped by cultures from around the world yet remains distinctly Asian at heart.
Sam Fielding, Tiger Global Brand Director, framed the range as a new flavour platform for the brand, with Peach Oolong and Yuzu Lime as the first two releases.
Where to buy Tiger Remix in Singapore
Tiger Remix is available now in single-can and 3-pack formats at 7-Eleven stores islandwide and on RedMart. A progressive rollout to major supermarkets, including FairPrice, Sheng Siong, Cold Storage and Giant, follows this November.

Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a Chinese-style mutton soup stall at 115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre , with eager customers already forming a queue before it even opens for the day. Erm, well, not quite for the whole day. It operates for just 2.5 hours (11am – 1.30pm) , 5 days a week . With a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 with a total of 369 reviews (at time of writing), it’s Singapore’s highest-rated mutton soup stall on Google Reviews .
A little voice in my head went, “It must be pretty darn good, eh?” This stall has also been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand for 9 consecutive years — that alone speaks volumes.
Naturally, my expectations were much higher than usual. As I stood in the queue, a rhythmic chopping sound echoed through the air, accompanied by a lady calling out and taking customers’ orders. As the fast-moving line gradually inched closer, the sounds that had been teasing my ears finally came into full view. From a conversation I couldn’t help but overhear, I gathered that the 2 ladies take turns swapping roles.
What to order at Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang
Most of the menu items come in 5 sizes, ranging from S$6 to S$10 , so there’s something suitable for every appetite. Just like the local saying goes, “Monkey see, monkey do.” I followed the lead of those queuing ahead of me and ordered the S$8 portion of the 羊杂 (mixed mutton) with a small bowl of Rice (S$0.40) .
For the price, I must say, the portion is pretty generous. There were pieces of mutton, 5 lamb balls, and lamb’s stomach bathed in a light brown soup, garnished with chopped Chinese celery.
The moment the soup hit my tongue, I was greeted by an unusual tingling sensation, accompanied by an almost siap siap mouthfeel. Its robust herbal profile brought to mind a hearty bowl of bak kut teh . It was definitely an acquired taste, and those who dislike herbal flavours may not appreciate it much. As someone who doesn’t mind herbal soups, I still felt that the flavour could be toned down a little to suit a wider audience.
The mutton here has got to be the Wagyu of its kind because, OMG, the meat was so tender that it barely required chewing, There was also no trace of unpleasant gaminess.
The lamb balls were firm yet smooth, and the overall texture reminded me of bouncy fishballs. It also packed a great flavour which wasn’t overly floury.
The stomach pieces were impeccably prepared, with a pleasantly clean flavour and none of that funky offal taste. I even found a couple of pieces of honeycomb tripe.
I then moved on to the S$8 bowl of 羊排骨汤 (mutton ribs soup) with rice as well. For S$8 , you’ll get about 7 to 8 substantial pieces of ribs. Much like the mutton from the previous dish, the rib meat was beautifully soft, with a pleasing balance of fat and lean meat.
For chilli lovers, I must say that this one is gentle enough for those who can’t handle too much heat, with a tangy profile reminiscent of the chilli commonly served alongside orh luak .
Who Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is best for
It’s perfect for herbal soup lovers who love something comforting for lunch. For those who avoid mutton like the plague because of its potential gaminess, Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a great place to start for its delicious, tender mutton; minus the strong taste.
How to get there?
115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre isn’t exactly near any MRT station. My recommendation would be to alight at Tiong Bahru MRT Station (EW17), get to the Opp Tiong Bahru Stn/Plaza bus stop, and board bus services that take you to Blk 116 .
Do we recommend Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang ?
If you love robust herbal flavours, then Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang will be up your alley. Mutton lovers who enjoy innards will appreciate the quality and softness of the lamb here. Oh, and I mustn’t forget the warm, friendly and efficient service here. It’s certainly the cherry on top!

Your Hogwarts letter might be a little late, but your next chance to shop for wizarding merchandise is just around the corner. House of Spells , a UK-based multi-fandom store, is opening its first outlet in Asia at 118 Mall KL , on 1 Dec 2026 , bringing collectibles inspired by Harry Potter , The Lord of the Rings and more to local fans.
Credit – House of Spells
Founded in 2016, the retailer brings together officially licensed merchandise from popular film, television and fantasy franchises. Potterheads can look forward to items inspired by Harry Potter and Fantastic Beasts , while fans of Game of Thrones , The Hobbit , Stranger Things , Marvel, DC Comics and Studio Ghibli will have plenty to browse too.
Credit – House of Spells
The collection includes magic wands , character figurines , themed apparel , jewellery , stationery , mugs , posters and other collectibles . You might find something to add to your display shelf, a souvenir featuring your favourite character or a gift for that friend who can recite the entire film from memory.
Credit – House of Spells
Beyond the merchandise, House of Spells aims to make the shopping experience part of the attraction. Its stores feature fantasy-inspired interiors, atmospheric lighting and interactive displays designed to evoke the fictional worlds behind the products. Staff who share an enthusiasm for these franchises are also available to help visitors explore the collections.
Credit – House of Spells
The brand operates several stores across the UK, including in London, Liverpool and Stratford-upon-Avon, as well as an outlet in New York City. Its Kuala Lumpur opening marks its first move into Asia, giving Malaysian fans a new place to discover officially licensed merchandise without travelling overseas.
Do note that the exact look and layout of the KL store have yet to be revealed.
Situated at 118 Mall within the Merdeka 118 precinct in KL, the opening House of Spells could be a fun addition to your next shopping trip , even if you only intend to browse. After all, resisting a collectible featuring your favourite character is one thing; having an entire store of them in front of you is another.

My first visit to Matsuya in Sapporo, Hokkaido, in 2019 was an unforgettable one. Just outside the entrance, my phone flashed an earthquake alert, and seconds later, the ground began shaking furiously beneath my feet. While the locals barely batted an eyelid, I froze in shock.
Thankfully, the piping-hot beef rice bowl waiting for me soon brought me back to my senses. Who knew that 7 years later, I’d be reunited with Matsuya, this time at Suntec City ’s basement in Singapore?
Located directly opposite Fish & Co., the eatery features self-service booths and spacious seating. The menu offerings mimic the ones you’ll find in Japan — an assortment of rice bowls including Unagi and Japanese curry .
Of course, we had to give the classic Gyumeshi Beef Bowl (S$5.50 for small) a try. There are also other sizes available – – – from Medium (S$5.90) to Double (S$10.90) . Savoury and tasty, the thin beef slices went well with the sweet onions and rice. Compared to its competitors, the beef at Matsuya offered a meatier bite with a leaner ratio of fat. We also added a Soft-Boiled Egg (+S$1.50) for maximum indulgence. Trust me, its worth it!
Our favourite was the Gyumeshi topped w/ Green Onion & Mentaiko Mayonnaise (S$8.50 for small) . Don’t be fooled by the intimidating sight of the green onion; it actually works! The combination of spring onions, creamy mentaiko , beef slices, and seaweed had multi layers of flavour that danced in my mouth.
We also tried the Soft Boiled Egg & Hamburg Steak with Tomato Sauce Set (S$13.50) which is known to be very popular in Japan. The meat was juicy and hearty, pairing perfectly with the tomato sauce and runny egg. The set comes with rice, miso soup, and a salad with mashed potato. To switch up the flavour, you can help yourself to the condiments on the table: Ponzu Citrus Sauce , Garlic Flavoured BBQ Sauce , Sesame Sauce , and more!
Come savour 60 years of hard work and dedication at Matsuya. For the best experience, we recommend ordering one variety of beef bowl each to share amongst your dining party.

Sake Matsuri, which bills itself as Southeast Asia’s largest sake festival, moves to Marina Bay Sands for its 13th edition on Saturday 28 and Sunday 29 November 2026, with regular tickets at S$60 for a three-hour tasting session . The festival takes over Hall C of the Sands Expo and Convention Centre, and tickets are on sale now.
The organiser puts the pour list at more than 500 sakes, shochu and artisanal spirits from over 100 breweries and distilleries. A craft beer festival, Japan HopFest SJ60 Edition, runs alongside on the same weekend.
The move follows a March 2026 edition at the F1 Pit Building and a November 2025 edition at Jewel Changi Airport, beside the Rain Vortex.
Guests at a past Sake Matsuri edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
How the sessions work
Each day has two sessions: 11am to 2pm and 4pm to 7pm. The halls close from 2pm to 4pm while the organiser turns them over, so tasting stops completely in that gap.
A regular ticket covers one session only. You cannot stay on into the next one. If you want a longer day, you buy a second session or go VIP. Late arrivals still get in, but the session ends on time, so a 6pm arrival for the 4pm slot gets an hour.
An exhibitor booth at a past edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
What a regular ticket gets you
The S$60 regular ticket includes a complimentary Sake Matsuri tasting glass, unlimited sampling across the 500-plus labels and entry to every festival zone, including a dedicated Spirits and Liquor Zone for Japanese gins, whiskies and shochu.
Masterclasses run by sake and shochu educators are included too. Seats are limited and you sign up in person at the Masterclass Lounge on the day. Bottles are on sale at the booths at festival prices.
There is also a food hall. Dishes there are priced separately from the ticket.
Tasting tables at a past edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
Bundles and VIP tickets
Groups get bundle pricing on regular tickets: five tickets for S$275, or eight for S$400.
VIP tickets cost S$128 for one person or S$248 for a couple. They cover the full day, both sessions, on your chosen date. On top of everything in the regular ticket, VIP holders get priority for masterclasses, a VIP Lounge for seating through the day and two-day access to Japan HopFest. The lounge stays open during the 2pm to 4pm break, but no food or drinks are served there.
All prices include GST.
A group at the Omu Nomu Craft Sake and Raw Bar booth at a past edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore
Before you buy
Tickets are final and non-refundable. They can be transferred to someone else if you contact the organiser’s support team at least 48 hours before the event with the new guest’s details.
The organiser strongly recommends buying online in advance and warns that past editions sold out before the festival weekend. Limited tickets might be available at the door.
Alcohol is served only to guests aged 18 and over, and staff can ask for photo ID at registration. Under-18s enter free with an adult but get no wristband or tasting glass. Designated drivers can enter with the ticketed guests they are driving, again without a wristband or glass. Paid parking is available at Marina Bay Sands.
An exhibitor at a past Sake Matsuri edition. Photo: Sake Matsuri Singapore

Orang Laut SG , the community group that has sold Southern Islander food mostly through weekend deliveries since 2020, opens its first walk-in cafe on Friday, 23 October, CNA Lifestyle reported. Called Terumbu, it runs at Chef X, #03-103/104 Clarke Quay Central, until 26 December.
Terumbu opens at Chef X on 23 October. Photo: Orang Laut SG
Terumbu is Malay for coral reefs. The pop-up is the 15th residency at Chef X, Far East Organization’s space for home-based and private-dining cooks to run a commercial restaurant for a fixed stint, with a professional kitchen, a dining room for up to 24 and mentoring from chef Isaac Tan of Commonwealth Concepts.
Two savoury dishes and island kueh
The menu is short. The Pulau Bowl is S$15.90 and puts three seafood dishes over jasmine rice with vegetables: asam pedas ikan karang (coral reef fish in a sour, spicy gravy), sotong hitam (squid cooked in its own ink) and sambal udang (stir-fried prawns in sambal).
The sotong hitam uses green-eyed squid, known as sotong nos, which is traditionally caught by line. The family picks it for the amount of ink it carries.
The second dish is bubur lambuk tenggiri, a Spanish mackerel porridge cooked with lemongrass, coconut milk and black pepper. It is S$11.90 with prawns or with squid, and S$13.90 with both.
Bubur lambuk tenggiri is S$11.90 with prawns or squid. Photo: Orang Laut SG
This is not the bubur lambuk handed out at mosques during Ramadan. On the islands it was an everyday dish, made by grinding leftover coral fish, bones and all, at a time when families had no fridge to keep the catch.
Dessert is kueh koleh-koleh and puteri salat, made by a former Pulau Bukom islander. The menu names coral fish without naming the species, because the fish changes with what islander fishermen bring in, including the few bubu (fish trap) makers who still go out to sea.
A family kitchen from Pulau Semakau
Founder Firdaus Sani is a fourth-generation Orang Pulau and Orang Laut whose family lived on Pulau Semakau for generations. They were moved to the mainland in 1977, and the island is now Singapore’s offshore landfill.
His mother does most of the cooking at Terumbu, with his aunt Rohaini running the floor and cousins helping out. The recipes come from his grandmother, Nenek Ninah, and are cooked by feel rather than by measurement.
The family runs Terumbu’s kitchen and floor. Photo: Orang Laut SG
Orang Laut SG started in 2020 as an Instagram page recording the memories, food and traditions of communities moved off the Southern Islands. Terumbu also has a small community gallery on the history of those islands.

BAO Fast Foods (BFF) is a new concept from London’s cult-favourite BAO . After a homecoming run in Taiwan, the pop-up will next land in Singapore at New Bahru from 11 November 2026 to 28 December 2026 .
But what exactly is this experience that is part fast food joint , part Asian convenience store ? Keep reading to find out more!
Credit: BAO
For those of you who enjoy exploring convenience stores when you’re overseas, especially in Asian countries like Taiwan, you will find the vibes here immaculate. At BFF, there will be a sense of familiarity with a distinct Taiwan flavour.
Credit: BAO
Expect shelves filled with Taiwanese comfort food and snacks , and a rotating selection of grab-and-go items. There will also be self-serve stations and sections featuring BAO’s merchandise .
From protein-packed bites like Egg Sandos and Marinated Eggs to high-fibre sides like “Fried Rice” Quinoa and Golden Kimchi , to sweet treats like Soy Puddings with tiramisu and banoffee toppings, you’ll have plenty to discover and revisit the pop-up for.
Credit: BAO
The signature item, however, is the Chicken Chopper (S$6.50) . Of course, when it comes to Taiwanese snacks, you must have fried chicken . And this is BFF’s take on the classic street food, perfected over 140 iterations.
You will notice that the chicken is cut with the bone left in place as a handle, making it easy to eat. By dipping the chicken in a soymilk batter and coating it in a tapioca starch mix, BFF ensures the meat stays juicy while having a light, crackly crust on the outside.
Flavours to look forward to include Original Crispy , Flame Glazed , and Master Scalded . The first is seasoned with Taiwanese white pepper, the second is flavoured with soy-garlic or mala hot honey glaze, and the third is dipped in a boiling soy-based master sauce with star anise and cinnamon.
Credit: BAO
For a more filling meal, you can order the Chicken Chopper as part of a rice box (S$7.95) , or pair it with Dan Dan Noodles (S$6.50) or Beef Cup Noodle (S$12.50) . Combos from S$9.50 are also available.
Credit: BAO
Another staple of Taiwanese food culture is tea ! And you will be able to find a selection of Taiwanese craft tea here at the BFF pop-up. Highlights include the nitro-infused Fluffy Natural Alishan Wintermelon (S$5.95) , the carbonated Orange Guava Beauty Tea (S$6.50) , and the rich Original Peanut Oatside Milk (S$6) .
If anything about this pop-up excites you, mark your calendars from 11 November to 28 December. It’s time to have a date at the convenience store!

Champagniac , Singapore’s dedicated Champagne festival, returns this weekend on 14 and 15 November for its second edition. It has moved from Jewel Changi Airport to the Supreme Court Terrace at National Gallery Singapore .
Credit: Champagniac 2025
Popping champagne in a former courthouse sounds like an objection, but I’m sure even lawyers won’t mind as long as their glasses are full.
Credit: National Gallery Singapore
Last year’s debut drew 1,400 people. The pitch hasn’t changed: Champagne for everyone, not only the person at dinner who smells “ brioche ” without being asked. Led by Yeo Xi Yang — he’s the 2022 Singapore National Sommelier Champion and runs Convivial , Southeast Asia’s first dedicated Champagne bar.
Champagne houses and growers pouring at Champagniac 2026
Credit: Champagniac 2025
For a festival trying to make Champagne more accessible, they’ve managed to bring in some seriously good producers. Big houses like Billecart-Salmon , Pommery , Deutz and Jacquesson sit alongside the growers Champagne nerds go misty-eyed over: Egly-Ouriet , Larmandier-Bernier , Pascal Doquet . Then there’s Selosse Pajon , made by the grand-nephew of Jacques Selosse and pouring in Singapore for the first time. If that surname means nothing to you, the queue at that booth will explain it.
There’s sparkling from outside Champagne, too. Gusbourne and Roebuck Estates are flying the English flag, and Spain’s Bodegas Balmoral is there with its traditional-method Edoné range. It’s a good chance to test whether you can tell English fizz from French. I wouldn’t bet money on it.
What the S$98 ticket covers
A regular ticket gets you one three-hour session, an SKLO Linear N.1 glass to take home (valued at S$69) and one tasting per booth. Note the “one.” Some of the highlighted bottles are premium pours, paid for with tokens sold on-site at S$5 each. The festival hasn’t published the token prices for individual bottles, so it’s hard to know how much extra you’ll end up spending.
Is the Champagniac VIP ticket worth it?
VIP is S$198 and capped at 60 people per session. What you’re really paying for is access to the Glass Room , a private lounge with seating and eight premium cuvées personally selected by Yeo. These are rarer bottles from houses at the fair that won’t be poured on the main floor. Three he’s flagged are the Egly-Ouriet V.P. Grand Cru , Henri Giraud MV20 Aÿ Grand Cru and Jacquesson Cuvée 743 .
For an extra S$100, that’s eight pours you won’t find elsewhere at the festival, plus somewhere to sit down. If you were already planning to burn through tokens, VIP makes sense. If you just want to discover a few new champagnes and have a good afternoon, the regular ticket is enough. VIPs can also pay another S$60 for the Grower package or S$80 for the Grande Maison package.
Credit: Champagniac 2025
Masterclasses, art and everything else
There are three masterclasses, each capped at 24 seats and booked separately on top of a festival ticket. On Saturday at 2.30pm, Alexandre Collard runs a Collard-Picard session (S$68), and everyone goes home with a demi-bottle. Sunday’s 2.30pm slot is Champagne A. Bergère, also S$68. The Henri Giraud class (S$88) is on Friday’s preview night, which is for National Gallery members only.
There’s also a Champagne-and-watercolour workshop with French artist D’Gers, where you get to paint your own postcard. It’s free for the first 30 people each session and S$10 after that. German artist Míru is showing new work, and three DJs are on the decks.

The line is part of Matchaya 3.0, under the name The Cloud Series. The ice is made by Kuramoto Ice in Kanazawa, Japan, and sourced through Kuramoto Ice Singapore, a family trade the brand traces to 1923. Each bowl is shaved into layers of sauce, cream and texture on that ice.
Five flavours on the Cloud Series
Five bowls sit on the kakigori menu, all marked as a Tiong Bahru exclusive:
• Signature Koicha Azuki: S$22++. Ceremonial matcha with azuki, red kidney beans, house-made granola and a delicate milk cream espuma.
• Burnt Butter Houjicha: S$18++. Roasted houjicha with brown butter cream, brown sugar jelly and a spiced Biscoff crumble.
• Chocolate Tiramisu: S$18++. Rich chocolate, ladyfingers and mascarpone cream with cacao chips, served alongside a double shot of espresso.
• Mango Coconut: S$20++. Mango compote and coconut cream espuma, with dried coconut and mango popping boba.
• Strawberry Yogurt: S$20++. Strawberry compote and fresh strawberries, with a tangy yogurt espuma and berry crisps.
Menu prices are subject to a 10 per cent service charge and GST. Matchaya’s homepage lists kakigori at 30 per cent off until 22 November. It does not set out further terms, so check in store before ordering.
How the bowls are built
Signature Koicha Azuki stacks koicha sauce with azuki paste and homemade matcha granola, then a Hokkaido milk espuma finished with koicha powder and red kidney beans.
Matchaya’s layer diagram for Signature Koicha Azuki. Image: Matchaya
Burnt Butter Houjicha holds houjicha sauce, brown sugar jelly and Biscoff crumble under a brown butter cream and a Hokkaido milk espuma. Chocolate Tiramisu uses a 73 per cent dark chocolate sauce with chocolate chips, ladyfingers and mascarpone cheese, and comes with a double shot of espresso on the side.
Matchaya’s layer diagram for Chocolate Tiramisu. Image: Matchaya
Strawberry Yogurt builds homemade strawberry sauce, strawberry compote, freeze-dried strawberry crumble and strawberry konjac balls under a yogurt espuma with lemon zest. Mango Coconut pairs mango sauce and mango compote with toasted coconut flakes and mango popping boba, then a coconut espuma with lemon zest and diced mango.
Matchaya’s layer diagram for Burnt Butter Houjicha. Image: Matchaya
Only at the Tiong Bahru flagship
The Tiong Bahru tea bar opens daily from 9.30am to 9.30pm. Havelock MRT is 7 minutes away, Outram 9 minutes and Tiong Bahru 13 minutes.
Matchaya’s menu marks the kakigori as a Tiong Bahru exclusive, and notes that the bowls are best enjoyed immediately.

Greenwood Fish Market VivoCity opens on 4 November 2026 at #01-188. Photo: Greenwood Fish Market
Greenwood Fish Market opens its first shopping mall outlet at VivoCity on 4 November 2026, 23 years after the seafood retailer and restaurant started on Greenwood Avenue in Bukit Timah. The Greenwood Fish Market VivoCity bistro sits at #01-188, next to TANGS and Tiong Bahru Bakery, and opens daily from 12pm to 10.30pm.
A bistro, not a third restaurant
VivoCity is the brand’s third address, after Bukit Timah and the Quayside Isle restaurant on Sentosa, which opened in 2015. It is also the first Greenwood Fish Market bistro. Founder David Lee told AsiaOne that half of the bistro menu carries Greenwood signatures, with the other half made up of new tapas, small plates and oshizushi, the pressed sushi. He also told AsiaOne that the outlet is a test bed for global franchising.
The bistro’s own recommendations are oysters, pastas, oshizushi and sharing plates. Alfresco seats are pet friendly, as they are at the two older outlets.
Set lunch and set dinner prices
The VivoCity set lunch runs Monday to Friday, 12pm to 5pm. Screenshot: Greenwood Fish Market, 21 October 2026
The three-course set lunch is S$29.95++ for a starter, a main and coffee or tea, from Monday to Friday, 12pm to 5pm. It does not run on public holidays or their eves. Starters include lobster bisque, assorted sashimi and hand-cut calamari. Mains include snapper fish and chips, prawn aglio, grilled barramundi and an Angus cheeseburger, while steak frites carries a S$12 supplement and pan-seared John Dory a S$10 supplement.
The four-course set dinner is S$45.95++ with a starter, a main, a dessert and a hot drink. Mains include a seafood marinara baked in a paper parcel, John Dory, steak frites and an A5 wagyu hamburg rice bowl. Black cod carries a S$14 supplement and USDA Choice ribeye a S$19 supplement.
Details
Greenwood Fish Market is not halal-certified, though the kitchen prepares dishes free of pork and alcohol when told in advance. Corkage is S$50++ for a bottle of wine and S$80++ for a bottle of spirits, and one bottle is waived for every bottle bought from the menu. VivoCity is linked to HarbourFront MRT station on the North East and Circle lines.

Chipotle Mexican Grill will open in Singapore in 2027
Image credit: @chipotle
Chipotle fans, here’s an update on that Singapore opening we told you about last year: the timeline’s officially been pushed back. Chipotle Mexican Grill has confirmed that its first Singapore restaurant will now open in 2027 , a year later than the 2026 date we first reported.

The delay comes as Chipotle finally kicks off its actual Asia debut, and Singapore, it turns out, isn’t first in line after all.

Chipotle opened its first-ever Asia outlet on 2 September 2026 , located along Gangnam-daero in Seoul’s Seocho-gu district. The restaurant runs through a joint venture named S&C Restaurants Holdings, formed with South Korean operator Sangmidang Holdings (formerly SPC Group), the same group behind Shake Shack, Paris Baguette, and Eggslut’s presence in Singapore.
For the uninitiated, Chipotle is a fast-casual Mexican chain known for its customisable burritos, tacos, and rice bowls. It began in 1993 as a lone restaurant in Denver, and has since expanded to include more than 4,200 outlets across the world.
Their menu is slated to be identical to those in the US and internationally. You can expect endless customisability with their build-your-own-meal concept, where they use fresh, responsibly sourced ingredients.
Image credit: @chipotle
You can get fully-stuffed Burritos as well as loaded Burrito Bowls , or if you like your meal light on carbs, you can choose to get their Salads, as well as their Tacos .
All their meats are responsibly raised, including Chicken , Pork Carnitas , Steak , and Barbacoa (braised beef) . They even have plant-based options, including the Sofritas , a plant-based protein, and Veggie , which comes with guacamole and beans.
Image credit: Chipotle
Chipotle will face stiff competition from existing fast-casual Mexican chains in Singapore, such as Australian-born Guzman Y Gomez, and homegrown brand Stuff’d. We’ll update this article once we get more information!

Three Bowls serves kolo mee at Whampoa Makan Place
Image credit: T greensake via Google Maps
If you want a Din Tai Fung-quality meal without its price tag, this hawker stall is worth checking out. Helmed by former Din Tai Fung chef Robin Lee, Three Bowls serves up East Malaysian fare at Whampoa Makan Place .
Paying homage to his roots, Chef Robin offers Sabah-style kolo mee, less com mon in Singapore than the Sarawak-style. The key difference lies in the darker, savoury soy sauce base, which gives Sabah-style noodles a richer, more robust flavour compared to the lighter, shallot oil-based Sarawak version.
Image credit: Wilfred Loy Yong Kang via Google Maps
Signature dishes are the Pork Chop Kolo Mee ($6.90) and Pork Chop Mee Soup ($6.90) , both featuring a Din Tai Fung-style fried pork chop.
Image credit: Patricia Lim via Google Maps
Alternatively, you can keep it simple with the Home Taste Kolo Mee ($4.50) and Home Taste Mee Soup ($4.50) , served with slices of char siew.
Other kolo mee options include Chicken Chop Kolo Mee ($6.50) , Fish Roll Fish Ball Mee ($4) , and Wanton Kolo Mee ($4) , available soup or dry.
If you opt for dry noodles, you can also customise your sauce. Choose from three options: White, a savoury shallot oil sauce; Black, a dark soy sauce with a hint of sweetness; or Red, a sweet char siew oil sauce.
Image credit: Zoey W via Google Maps
Another specialty of Three Bowls is the Homemade Knife-Cut Noodles ($6.90) , featuring chef Robin’s hand-pulled noodles—said to have a chewy texture and topped with fish balls and meat balls.
While the store is relatively new, it’s already built a solid fanbase with long queues every day. If you love the iconic Ding Tai Fung pork chop, then you need to give this a go.
